Bhalchandra Nemade
Beginning with his debut novel Kosala, Nemade brought new dimensions to the world of Marathi literature.
In 2013, Nemade published his magnum opus titled Hindu: Jagnyachi Samruddha Adgal (Marathi: हिंदू: जगण्याची समृद्ध अडगळ) which is regarded as his masterpiece.
Nemade is a recipient of the Sahitya Akademi Award as well as the Jnanapith Award, the highest literary honour in India.

After doing his matriculation, he moved to Pune, and received his BA from Fergusson College in Pune and MA in Linguistics from Deccan College in Pune and English Literature from the Mumbai University in Mumbai.
From 1973 to 1986, he taught English at Marathwada University in Aurangabad.
In 1987, he was appointed as professor and head of department of English at Goa University.
In 1991, he joined Mumbai University, from where he retired as the Gurudeo Tagore Chair for comparative literature studies.
Sangvikar, the narrator in Kosala, uses everyday Marathi spoken in rural Maharashtra and his worldview also reflects that held by residents of rural Maharashtra.
Kosala is a chronological autobiographical narration, yet it employs certain innovative techniques.
Kosla is extensively translated into various languages including English, Hindi, Gujarati, Kannada, Assamese, Punjabi, Bengali, Urdu, Oriya, et al.
After Kosala, Nemade presented a different protagonist, Changadev Patil, through his four novels Bidhar (Marathi: बिढार), Hool (Marathi: हूल), Jarila (Marathi: जरीला) and Jhool (Marathi: झूल).
Another tetralogy begins with Hindu – Jagnyachi Samruddha Adgal (Marathi: हिंदू – जगण्याची समृद्ध अडगळ) in 2010 having Khanderao, the archaeologist as its protagonist.
Sangvikar is mercurial, Patil is more realistic, whereas Khanderao's consciousness moves across 5000 years to Indus Valley culture in the Hindu tetralogy.

As a critic, Nemade's contribution rests in initiating Deshivad, a theory that negates globalisation or internationalism, asserting the value of writers' native heritage, indicating that Marathi literature ought to try to revive its native base and explore its indigenous sources.
Winner of the Sahitya Akademi Award, he was conferred with Padma Shri in 2011 by Government of India.

Dnyaneshwari

The Dnyaneshwari (Marathi: ज्ञानेश्वरी) (IAST: Jñānēśvarī), also called Jnanesvari, Jnaneshwari or Bhavartha Deepika, is a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita written by the Marathi saint and poet Sant Dnyaneshwar in 1290 CE.
The Dnyaneshwari interprets the Bhagavad Gita in the Advaita Vedanta tradition of Hinduism.
The text is the oldest surviving literary work in the Marathi language, one that inspired major Bhakti movement saint-poets such as Eknath and Tukaram of the Varkari (Vithoba) tradition.

According to Pradhan and Lambert, the reliable dating of Dnyaneshwari to 1290 CE is based on textual and corroborative reference to the Yadava king Ramadeva as well as the name of the scribe and the samvat of its completion.
Scholars generally accept that this version is most faithful one, and this edition was identified in 1909 by V.
Each of its 9,000 verses consists of four lines (quarters) called an ovi (a form of Marathi meter).
The text reverentially includes the names of numerous Hindu gods and goddesses from Vaishnavism, Shaivism, and Shaktism traditions, as well as Vedic ones such as Saraswati (Sharada).
The last line of many of its verses include the characteristic "Jnanadeva says" or "Says Jnanesvara".

Ramcharitmanas (Devanagari: रामचरितमानस rāmacaritamānasa), is an epic poem in the Awadhi language, composed by the 16th-century Indian bhakti poet Tulsidas (c.
Tulsidas was a great scholar of Sanskrit, but due to limited accessibility of the language, he chose to write it in the vernacular, Awadhi, making his work more accessible to the general public.
Tradition has it that Tulsidas had to face much criticism from the Sanskrit scholars of Varanasi for being a vernacular poet.

In May 2024, during the tenth meeting of the Memory of the World Committee for Asia and the Pacific, the Ramcharitamanas manuscripts were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Regional Register.
One manuscript was authored by Tulsidas, and the other was written in Arabic in the 18th century, showcasing the text's appeal in West Asia and other parts of the world.
The exact date is stated within the poem as being the ninth day of the month of Chaitra, which is the birthday of Rama or Rama Navami.
The core of the work is considered by some to be a poetic retelling of the events of the Sanskrit epic Ramayana by Valmiki.
Rama was the crown prince of Ayodhya and is considered in Hindu tradition as the seventh avatar of Vishnu.
The epic poem is, therefore, also called Tulsikrit Ramayana (literally, The Ramayana composed by Tulsidas).
Tulsidas compared the seven Kāndas of the epic to seven steps leading into the holy waters of Lake Manasarovar "which purifies the body and the soul at once".
The first two parts, Bāl Kāṇḍ (Childhood Episode) and Ayodhyā Kāṇḍ (Ayodhya Episode), make up more than half of the work.
The other parts are Araṇya Kāṇḍ (Forest Episode), Kiśkindhā Kāṇḍ (Kishkindha Episode), Sundar Kāṇḍ (Pleasant Episode), Laṅkā Kāṇḍ (Lanka Episode), and Uttar Kāṇḍ (Later Episode).
The work is primarily composed in the Chaupai metre (four-line quatrains), separated by the Doha metre (two-line couplets), with occasional Soratha and various Chhand metres.

Nirala's father, Pandit Ramsahaya Tripathi, was a government servant and was a tyrannical person.
Nirala was educated in the Bengali medium at Mahishadal Raj High School at Mahishadal, a princely state in Purba Medinipur.
Subsequently, he shifted to Lucknow and thence to village Gadhakola of Unnao district, to which his father originally belonged.
Growing up, he gained inspiration from personalities like Ramakrishna Paramhansa, Swami Vivekananda, and Rabindranath Tagore.
After his marriage at the age of 15, Nirala learned Hindi at the insistence of his wife, Manohara Devi.
After a bad childhood, Nirala had a few good years with his wife.
But this phase was short-lived as his wife died when he was 22, and later his daughter Saroj also died.
Nirala lost half of his family, including his wife and daughter, in the 1918 Spanish flu influenza outbreak.
All these may have played a role in making him a patient of schizophrenia in his later life and he was admitted to Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi.
His initial poetry reflects the Bengali Renaissance and Contextual Modernism, aligning with the mystical-romanticism, or Chhayavad, that emerged in Hindi literature in the subsequent decades.
Over time, Nirala evolved a distinctive style, diverging from his early influences and exploring a range of literary genres, including free verse.
Nirala's poetry illustrated a profound connection with the living spirits of nature.

While the concept of nature as a manifestation of the absolute was common among Chhayavadi poets, Nirala uniquely portrayed the natural world, not only as a female but also as a fundamentally erotic entity, as seen in works such as Sandhyā Sundarī, Jūhī kī kalī, and Yāminī jāgī.
His poem Rām kī śakti Pūjā explores selfless action through the struggles of Rama, serving as an allegory for broader themes of resilience and social struggle.
Its subdued treatment and pensive dignity elevated it to epic stature, and it remained one of the finest elegies in Hindi literature.
Themes of minority subjectivity and social critique are also prominent in Nirala's prose writings, such as Kullī bhāṭ and Caturī Camār.
His anthology of songs, titled Gītikā and published in 1936, features a collection of his musical works.

Vyankatesh Madgulkar
Venkatesh Digambar Madgulkar (5 April 1927 – 28 August 2001) was one of the most popular Marathi writers of his time.
His father was in the employment of the government of the Aundh princely state.
When Madgulkar was in his teens, he left home and joined a group of nationalists fighting for India’s freedom from the British Raj.
For these activities, the British government banned him as a criminal for two years.
Though he had never finished his high school education, but he passed vernacular final Marathi 7th exam with good marks.
Madgulkar also had an aptitude for sketching and painting, so he went to Kolhapur to take painting lessons.
In 1948, when he was 21, he became a journalist and, two years later, he moved to Mumbai where he had the opportunity to write scripts for a few Marathi movies.
In 1955, Madgulkar took a job in Pune in the rural programming department of All India Radio.
His 1954 novella Bangarwadi (बनगरवाडी) was translated in several languages, including English, German, and Hindi.
His novel Wawtal (वावटळ) was translated into English, Kannada and also in Russian by Raduga Publishers.
A movie based on Bangarwadi was made under the direction of Amol Palekar.
The same year, he presided over Marathi Sahitya Sammelan, which was held at Ambajogai.
